summary: Cast-iron lighthouse of 1846 on a private Lake Champlain island off Burlington; the navigation light moved to a steel tower in 1954.

structures.note: Four cast-iron rings, 30 ft (9.1 m) to the lantern. Replaced a conical brick tower of 1826.
Automatic light on a 60-ft steel skeleton tower (LighthouseFriends); replaced in 2003 (New England Lighthouses).
New skeleton tower carrying the navigation light (New England Lighthouses).

access.note: Private island, not open to the public (USLHS). Reached by boat. Visitors should not land.

facts.agency: Private owner (island sold at auction in 1956)

events.note: Station established 1826 (USLHS); LighthouseFriends gives 11 May 1826 as the first lighting.
Conical brick tower, 30 ft (9.1 m), with ten lamps and reflectors.
Inspection found the tower much out of repair; $500 requested (as quoted by LighthouseFriends).
Four cast-iron rings replaced the 1826 brick tower.
Fourth-order Fresnel lens: USLHS gives 1853; LighthouseFriends gives 1856. Unresolved.
Congress appropriated $2,500 for a lighthouse and buoy depot.
Old wharf extended 80 feet; combined boathouse and buoy shed built at the inshore end.
Northwest gale carried away 30 feet of the dock.
Automatic light on a 60-ft (18.3 m) steel skeleton tower replaced the iron lighthouse's light.
Iron tower's light discontinued (USLHS); the navigation light moved to the steel tower.
Sold at auction; highest of eight bids was $7,000 (LighthouseFriends).
Keeper's house badly damaged or destroyed by a camper's fire.
Reconstruction of the keeper's house begun, using salvaged bricks.
New steel skeleton tower installed; the navigation light moved to it.

corrections.why: The 1826 structure was a conical brick tower (LighthouseFriends, New England Lighthouses). The cast-iron tower dates to 1846 (USLHS: tower established 1846).

The navigation light has been on a steel skeleton tower since 1954 and on a newer one since 2003 (New England Lighthouses). The iron tower is no longer the navigation light, so 'inactive' may describe only that tower. Check the current Light List before changing it.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's 1826 date and cast-iron material apply to different towers: the 1826 tower was brick, and the cast-iron tower was built in 1846.

notes_for_editor: Unresolved: (1) lens year, 1853 (USLHS) against 1856 (LighthouseFriends). The story states both. (2) Focal height: the record's 18.3 m (60 ft) matches the 60-ft steel tower of 1954; USLHS gives 93 ft above mean high water (28.3 m) for the iron light. Check against the Light List. (3) Range: the record has 7 nm; LighthouseFriends quotes an older description of the light as visible for fifteen miles. Not used in the story. (4) Keeper dates: Perry 1905-1935 (USLHS, which agrees with the Perry lines in the roster) against 1903-1937 (New England Lighthouses); Joseph Aubin 1936-1943 (USLHS) against 1937-1941 (New England Lighthouses). The story states the Perry disagreement. (5) Dwelling: USLHS says brick; New England Lighthouses says a stone dwelling of 1863; LighthouseFriends describes a white two-story dwelling attached to the tower. Not used in the story. (6) LighthouseFriends and New England Lighthouses are secondary. The 1838 Platt report, the 1841 letter and the 1904 Boston Globe account were read only as quoted by LighthouseFriends, and the story attributes them to LighthouseFriends (the Globe account is 'as LighthouseFriends quotes it'). (7) The 1956 buyer: LighthouseFriends names a Burlington law firm (Fayette & Deschenes) as the highest bidder; New England Lighthouses names a lawyer and state senator. Left unnamed in the story, as are the family members who later owned the island. (8) Photos were not added. The Wikidata photo is on the record. (9) Keeper count: the USLHS roster prints 18 principal-keeper lines; Malachi Corning appears twice (1829-1841 and 1843-1844), so the story says 18 entries for 17 different men. (10) Fiscal years: the wharf estimates are in the Commissioner's reports for the fiscal years ended 30 June 1918 (scan 385, printed 71; No. 38, $150,000) and 30 June 1920 (scan 583, printed 85; No. 56, $150,000). The 1919 and 1921 estimates for the same wharf are not used. (11) The 1918 gale: LighthouseFriends dates the damage to 1 December 1918 (Perry's letter, 3:30 a.m.); New England Lighthouses says 'in 1918'. (12) The 1891 appropriation quote is checked against the cached 1891-92 Light-House Board text, where the line break hyphen rejoins to 'lighthouse'. (13) The Coast Guard's 4,000 sq ft and right of entry come from LighthouseFriends only.
